utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Jordash, if you're ready, you may start your closing argument. But Mr. Groome is on his feet. I don't think he wants to prevent you from doing it, but to raise another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it relates to a written document that the Stanisic Defence indicated it intended to hand to the Chamber in file. Is it -- if it is still their intention to do that I would want to address the Chamber on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is our intention and can I just -- maybe I can shortcut things a little but just indicating what our approach was going to be. We prepared a table which are corrections of the Prosecution's closing brief, which include such things as miscitations and failures to put before Your Honours the witness's retractions, and so on. It is not, we will say, submissions. It's corrections which are material to a fair assessment to Mr. Stanisic' criminal responsibility. What I was hopping to do -- we sent it to the Prosecution because we understood that it might be a little controversial, we wanted their position and we were going to ask Your Honours for some time at the end of the speeches perhaps tomorrow to argue the point if there was any opposition from Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, Mr. Jordash apparently is suggesting that we should wait and at a later stage that you have a possibility to make submissions that Mr. Jordash will further explain. May I take it that the concern is that there is an additional round of argument claimed by the -- or is there anything else involved?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. And as long as before it is handed to the Chamber that I have a full opportunity to address the Chamber on it. I'm happy to -- to defer that till the end of the closing submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we proceed as suggested by Mr. Jordash and agreed upon by Mr. Groome. Mr. Jordash, I think you have two and a half hours. I would split that up in two sessions of 75 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Today in the main, we will address certain aspects of the Prosecution's closing brief and their approach to this case. Tomorrow, we will address their closing remarks of yesterday. We say Mr. Stanisic should be acquitted of all charges. He should walk out of this courtroom as a free man without a stain on his reputation. We urge the Court to reject the Prosecution case and allow him to return to his community, to enjoy the peace that he helped to secure. The case against him is not even reasonable, let alone proven beyond a reasonable doubt. Despite that, we do not suggest it was wrong to prosecute Mr. Stanisic. We know that Mr. Stanisic's proximity to the events during the indictment period raises a degree of suspicion. But we submit that this trial has amply demonstrated that that suspicion tells us little other than Mr. Stanisic was the Serbian chief of security in a time of war. It was impossible to be an effective chief of State Security during a bloody civil war without being proximate to the events. A skilled prosecutor and a handful of self-serving witnesses can use that fact to raise a prima facie case, but strain as they might, that suspicion cannot be transformed to proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The evidence is just too equivocal, too unreliable, and too absent on critical issues to discharge that burden of proof. In 1991, Mr. Stanisic was an assistant in the State Security of Serbia, and from 1992 to 1998, he was the head. Of course, he was involved in the war. Of course, he was not without influence. Of course, he attended meetings with many of the critical players, including Milosevic, Martic, Babic, Karadzic, Mladic, and so on. Of course, he could not publicly express his disagreement with government policy. Of course, in meetings he may have had to align himself with aspects of the Serbian government policy. This much we knew from the outset of the trial. We know that these facts raised legitimate questions. But these questions have not been fairly addressed by the Prosecution in the conduct and closing of their case, nor have the answers proven a case beyond a reasonable doubt. Rather than conceding a single inch of this extravagant case the Prosecution pushed on, claiming that all aspects of its case have been proven beyond a reasonable doubt. As we shall argue in these closing remarks, by refusing to make a single concession and otherwise attempting to mask the collapse of their case on pivotal issues, the Prosecution rides over Mr. Stanisic's presumption of innocence. Meeting with Milosevic and other Serbian leaders, providing security related information to the Serbian government, communicating with Karadzic, Martic, and others to obtain the best information, being a channel of communication between the leaders on issues pertaining to the security of Serbia fell squarely within the purview of his job. The Prosecution must prove that Mr. Stanisic's proximity to the leadership and these activities were not in pursuance of his lawful duties and they must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that they were in furtherance of crime. Instead, the Prosecution continues to advance without providing the assistance to the Court on these critical distinctions. Everything Mr. Stanisic did was in furtherance of crime. All his DB operatives were criminals. Every effort he made to secure the security of Serbia was illegitimate, every motive was bad. He is responsible for all the supplies, each Serb force and all the paramilitaries in one way or another. The Prosecution has long since abandoned the pursuit of a reasonable case let alone one that allows that Mr. Stanisic had a legitimate and vital, non-political task that involved the protection of millions of Serbian citizens. Serbia required a functioning security system. It required state security. This is the starting point, we suggest, for Your Honours when one considers the presumption of innocence. It is not enough to point at presence in the field or other similar evidence consistent with the state security's tasks and with a wink and a nod urge Your Honours to conclude that these legitimate activities must have been a cover for something else. Of course Mr. Stanisic could have resigned his job. He would have avoided the challenges of this criminal trial that have disrupted his life, maligned his reputation and undermined his health, but that would have been to take an easy road. And we say as forcefully as we can: Remaining in his job was the fit and proper and principled thing to do. The war was not his priority but it was his concern. And as we shall outline over the next two and a half hours, in a time of madness and ethnic hatred he stood as one of the few voices of reason. We say the evidence shows he has never been a nationalists. He has never hated non-Serbs or believed in the superiority of Serbs. He has never believed in power for power's sake. At a time when leaders on all sides were marching to war, he, alone of all the leaders, reached out to the international community to assist them to bring this terrible conflict to an end. From the outset he did not even believe it was possible to keep Yugoslavia together, let alone create a Greater Serbia. He does believe in a Greater Serbia, but knows that's not about land or territory but about people, values, and being a member of a progressive international community. The evidence shows this to be true, and the Prosecution has failed to prove otherwise. As we note at paragraph 1258 of our closing brief, joint criminal enterprise is not an open-ended concept that permits convictions based on guilt by association or by otherwise collectivising culpability. Proof of the significance of the accused's contribution is required to prove that the accused shared the intent to pursue the crimes and the criminal purpose. That requires holding tight to fundamental trial principles, the careful sifting of evidence and prudent application of the burden of proof. Unfortunately, the Prosecution has abandoned these fundamentals. Having watched over the Defence phase of this trial, the Prosecution justify the admission of an unprecedented amount of new evidence on the alter of contextualization. One might have expected that their final submissions would have been meticulous in ensuring that Your Honours have the salient evidence brought to your attention. On the contrary, we submit, the Prosecution's final brief does everything it can to avoid the totality of the evidence and the inconvenience of fact and truth. As slide 2 shows or outlines, this closing speech will be divided into three parts. If we could turn to that now. Part 1 will discuss the thematic problems inherent in the Prosecution's approach to the individual liability of Mr. Stanisic. In this part, we will address the ways in which the Prosecution's approach seeks to reverse the burden and lower the standard of proof. This part of the speech is supplemented by the table, which we discussed a moment ago. To ask a man -- sorry. To ask a Court to remove a man's liberty for the rest of his life is an act of utmost solemnity. To do so without the accurate recitation of evidence or a reasonable approach to the facts will not enhance the reputation of this Tribunal. Part 2 of the speech will address the fundamental premise of the Prosecution's case against Mr. Stanisic that he was the principal co-ordinator or channel of communication between Milosevic, Martic, Babic, Hadzic, and Karadzic. According to paragraph 46 of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, Stanisic was Milosevic's number 2. In order to fulfil this function he is alleged to have co-ordinated the crimes with these regional leaders. This is how the theory goes. He managed to exert such authority over the military event, deploy Arkan into the SBWS and elsewhere, deploy the Red Berets, he provided, it is alleged, significant assistance to the war effort, deploy the Skorpions, plan the Vukovar operations, and so on and so forth. We will demonstrate how the evidence has fallen manifestly short of even proving this originating premise. Part 3 of the speech will focus very briefly on Mr. Stanisic as a man and as a professional. Despite the layperson's belief, because that is what it is, that in times of horrific crimes all those in leadership positions must be responsible. The evidence shows that it was possible to remain in situ as the head of state of security, swim against the tide and help in often intangible ways to ameliorate the pain and suffering. Of course, with some actions this is easily demonstrated. Negotiating the release of the UNPROFOR hostages in 1995, the rescue of the French pilot, these are obvious examples of good that can be done in the midst of terrible crimes. Less obvious but no less important are the incremental steps that Stanisic took that -- that paved the way for a more secure Serbia or the effort spent calming the fevered mind of the extremists such as Babic or Martic, individuals determined to take their people to hell and back. The quiet diplomacy, the late nights studying the actions of criminals, the strategic dismantling of criminal networks, his efforts cajoling Babic to sign the Vance Plan, his secret co-operation with vital international partners from 1991 onwards as the Balkans burnt in ethnic fury. We say he kept his head when all about were losing theirs. These acts are representative of his professional and personal disposition and pivotal to an assessment of his mens rea. We submit these acts have been proven and not the allegations or fabrications, the rumours propounded by unreliable Prosecution witnesses. These are the acts which form the springboard from which Your Honours might judge his true intent. Part 3 covers this subject. If we can turn to slide 3. This outlines part 1 of the speech. The Prosecution's inappropriate approach to individual criminal responsibility. Respectfully, we submit, that the Prosecution's approach in this case is wrong in principle. It invites the attribution of guilt by association and supposition. The case against Stanisic in almost all respects lacks direct evidence. The case rests upon a framework of testimony provided by 92 quater witnesses and an attempt to link Stanisic to Simatovic and others through circumstantial evidence that consists largely of multiple hearsay and speculation. According, the Prosecution appeared to have lapsed into employing various strategies which we urged the Trial Chamber to examine with care. If we could turn to slide 4. The first such strategy is asserting that the accused worked in secrecy or in the shadows. Playing on the Hollywood depiction of the State Security Service and perhaps even a nod to the post September 11th illegal practices of the CIA and MI6, the Prosecution seeks to preserve certain aspects of its JCE case. Slide 4 provides a selection of illustrations from the Prosecution's brief showing the attempt to conceal the paucity of evidence in support of the case. This narrative seeks to reduce the evidential burden by asserting without real support that Stanisic's action were undertaken secretly. The last assertion on slide 4 is a good example. Until the Prosecution's closing brief, the Prosecution had not alleged that Stanisic controlled the Skorpions secretly. On the contrary, in their 2007 pre-trial brief, paragraph 81, the Prosecution alleged, and I quote: "The Skorpions also received ID booklets indicating membership of the DB." Presumably these cards were to be shown publicly to provide them with the status and privilege of a DB-sponsored unit. Having watches Stoparic's evidence collapse and JF-024 and JF-029 failed to come up to proof and having belatedly realised that the DB never had their own ID cards, they now assert that the accused secretly controlled the Skorpions. This approach is intellectually circular. Of course, Mr. Stanisic acted in secret. He worked in the State Security Service. But as with protective measure in this case or cases at the ICTY, certain information is denied to the public and for good reason. However, as with this trial, we in this room, the stenographers, the translators, the Prosecution, Registry, and Defence are privy to the so-called secret information. Likewise, in Mr. Stanisic's case, the public may not have known but the insiders knew. If they didn't know, it's because Mr. Stanisic was not acting as the Prosecution allege. Whilst not listed on slide 4, let's consider for a moment the thesis advanced by Babic. Babic is the only Prosecution witness who gave evidence about the existence of a parallel structure in the Krajina. Babic claimed that the state security controlled that structure and from the end of June 1991 onwards, had overall control of the events at the time, and I quote: "This parallel structure bypassed the de jure civilian and military chain of command, provoked reaction and fear amongst the Serbs which spiralled up to intolerance, violence and essentially war." Babic indirectly supported this methodology by failing to speak out against their methods, according to his plea agreement. The problem with that thesis is that there is so little evidence to support it. Whilst there is evidence, unconvincing evidence, we say, of a leadership role for Stanisic in the creation of Golubic and the early financing of the Krajina police, it falls subsequently short of suggesting any planning or command role that might start to look like a dominant military or political power structure forcing the furtherance of a criminal purpose against the will of a prostrate Babic. The evidence is just not there. Of course, it was not possible for Stanisic to control all the military activity in the Krajina without anyone but Babic observing this to be the case. It is not possible for 5.000 men to have been commanded by a DB command unit without anyone knowing this to be true. Had there been truth to this, the insiders would know. There lies a misleading contradiction at the heart of the Prosecution case. At the same time as alleging secrecy they allege that Mr. Stanisic acted completely recklessly. They allege that he sent blue MUP special purpose trucks into the Krajina with blue registration plates, police registration plates; that he personally met a witness to hand over bags of cash to finance the Krajina police; that he created a paramilitary group with flamboyant red berets that fanned out to the war zones setting up 26 training bases and otherwise forming the backbone of the war effort. At paragraph 17 of their closing brief, they alleged he met routinely with Serb leaders in the Krajina, ensuring their access to JCE members in Belgrade; that he arrived Dalj in mid-September 1991 screaming in public with regard to the failure of the SBWS leadership to liberate Vukovar; that he along with five other men arranged hundreds and thousands of tonnes of military hardware through Prodanic and the association of the Serbs to the RS and the RSK who would meet practically on a daily basis, and yet the Prosecution alleged that Stanisic worked in the shadows. It is it simply not possible to be responsible for delivering hundreds of thousands of weapons over the indictment period as alleged by 92 quater witness B-179 without people knowing -- without, sorry, five people knowing, according to B179. Mladic and Milovanovic would at least have known. Instead, as we shall see shortly, there is instead a single reference in the Mladic notebooks of a single delivery by Prodanic, the chief of the 8th Administration, and as we can see if we examine that entry those weapons were not for the VRS. Mladic did not even have Stanisic's phone number until 1995. Milovanovic met Stanisic in 1993 and thought he was a waiter. Is it possible to send Dragan or Crnogorac to Brcko in 1991 to train the Bosnian Serb forces as part of a 28 elite trainer project without the authorities in the RS knowing that they were coming and they came from Stanisic and Stanisic wanted it to happen and was working with those VRS members? In short, when Stanisic or the DB was involved, it was known, not by the public, but by the military intelligence, by those receiving the supplies, by a multitude of mid-ranking men who had to assist with the arrangements. If the Prosecution after pouring through the 9 million documents in its archives, cannot build a case against Mr. Stanisic it's not because he was working in the shadows. It's because it's not true. If we could turn to slide 5. The second strategy employed the Prosecution to reduce their evidentiary burden is the invitation to disregard the Appeals Chamber's requirements that the contour of the criminal purpose be defined and proven beyond a reasonable doubt. This includes defining the manner in which JCE members used perpetrators, the names of these perpetrators, and how it is alleged that their crimes fall within the common purpose. As slide 5 indicates, only this will prevent the JCE doctrine from overreaching on lapsing into guilt by association. In this case, the Prosecution failed to provide the accused with consistent information concerning the case against him. Principally, regarding the non-JCE members, he is alleged to have used to furthered the common criminal purpose. As we note in the first section of our closing brief, their original case of 28 elite trainers, the core of the unit has collapsed. Instead of admitting this fact, the Prosecution sought to build a new case. If we could turn to slide 6. Defence has consistently objected to the manner in which the Prosecution attempted to build its new case. Slide 6 contains examples of the Defence complaints regarding the Prosecution's unwillingness to identify the non-JCE members used by Stanisic. If we could turn to slide 7. Slide 7 contains a snap-shot of the law with regard to the Prosecution's responsibility to provide the names of the perpetrators of crimes. In short, and as stated at paragraph 32 of the 2009 Karadzic decision listed in the slide: "The identity of the alleged physical perpetrators constitute information relevant for the preparation of an effective defence." The ICTY Prosecution in that case agreed that it should provide this information to the Defence "in so far as it has" such information. The Trial Chamber is aware of the Defence concern about this issue. Until this point, the Trial Chamber found the Defence argument that the Prosecution would rely upon individuals introduced in the main through so-called DB personnel files as speculative. We submit this is no longer the case. The next slide should not be broadcast to the public. Could we turn to slide 8, please. As we can see from slide 8, slide 8 contains a list of 48 non-JCE members or physical perpetrators including the core 28 that we began this case with, but we accept the Prosecution provided some notice. The next slide, slide 9 - confidential, please - by contrast contains the list of 60 alleged perpetrators or non-JCE members contained in Annex A of the Prosecution closing that have been introduced into this trial without proper notice. There are additional alleged perpetrators throughout the brief which are not in Annex A. Footnote 851 is a good example of alleged perpetrators introduced similarly late. Rather than admitting the lack of notice, or the need for notice, I should say, like the Karadzic Prosecution team and then attempting as they must to satisfy the Trial Chamber that the Defence has not been prejudiced, the Prosecution have recategorised the issue. Annex A of the Prosecution brief is an invitation to the Trial Chamber to disregard the tools test for a watered-down version revolving around a new significant relationship threshold. Or allow me to put that threshold into the logic of the Prosecution's submissions yesterday. Your Honours can be satisfied that Kostic, Kojic and all those who had any relationship with the DB at any time or any place was at the behest of Mr. Stanisic because, and I quote: "Their actions were carried out in accordance with how Stanisic intended to use the Serbian DB to further the JCE." The Prosecution, they said yesterday, does not need to produce evidence of an order directly from Stanisic in order to meet its burden of proof. In other words, you can conclude that those with a significant relationship to the DB was acting at Mr. Stanisic's behest because the DB was acting in furtherance of the common purpose and we know that those people were acting in furtherance of the common purpose because the DB was acting in furtherance of the common purpose, a wonderful circularity that removes the need to prove any act by Stanisic other than maintaining his post in the DB. Annex A should in fact be called: Index of persons with a significant relationship to the Serbian DB, also known as the 28 core. Plus: Alleged perpetrators we want to introduce into this trial without proper notice. Or perhaps something like: Index of men we want to use to incriminate in some unspecified way but without respecting JCE law. If the Prosecution does not accept this, perhaps in their reply they might enlighten us with what the Chamber should do with persons who they say had a significant relationship with the DB who had the tools in that list or who, in the Prosecution's words of yesterday, are other relevant individuals, their understanding of the applicable law that must be used to assess whether their crimes, if found proven, were within the common purpose. Any actions in furtherance of crimes or crimes committed by men who have not been defined at the outset as tools with notice provided as to how they were used and by whom should be, we submit, dismissed from this case. The third strategy, we submit, employed by the Prosecution is to conflate the DB's intelligence work with crime. It amounts to an assertion that the presence of DB operatives in the field must mean that they were engaged in crime at the behest of the accused. It is an invitation to the Trial Chamber to require proof from the accused that they were not engaged in crime at his behest, a reversional of proof by another name. The most obvious examples of this attempt to obscure these critical distinctions are with regard to the SBWS crime base. At paragraphs 49 and 50 of the Prosecution's final brief, and I quote, they say: "Stanisic embedded MUP DB operatives in the SAO SBWS government and other positions throughout the region to further the JCE's common purpose. MUP DB operatives Kojic and Kostic were particularly instrumental." At paragraph 49 and 50, they suggest: "Their activities were not limited to collecting intelligence; rather, Kojic, Kostic and other DB members were involved in 'other work.'" What may we ask was this other work? It has not been, we suggest, defined and if the tools test is to be satisfied, it must be. Let us look briefly at Kojic. Despite not mentioning this alleged perpetrator in the indictment or pre-trial brief he has played an inordinately large role in this case. The Prosecution want you to accept that his other work was at the behest of Stanisic, not because they can show this to be the case, not because they can point to a single order or instruction that came from Stanisic, but because he was engaged as an intelligence operative by the DB. If we can turn to slide 10, please. The dangers of this approach are obvious but worth highlighting. Slide 10 is a quote by Witness Bogunovic, a Prosecution witness. Witness Bogunovic demonstrates that even though the Prosecution seek to obscure the critical distinctions between intelligence gathering and other work that is capable of being considered in furtherance of crime, those on the ground did make those distinctions, as the witness noted: "Well, the way I saw it at the time, it seems that people who were appointed," referring to Kojic, "were those who would certainly keep them," authorities in Belgrade, "posted at all times about what we were doing in the government and what was happening in the area." Bogunovic identify the reasonable inference that in the absence of evidence to suggest otherwise raises a reasonable doubt. If we could turn to slide 11, please. Slide 11 demonstrated further the dangers of the Prosecution's approach. Kojic's other work at this critical time was at the behest of others such as Simovic, the minister of defence, ordering Kojic personally in every aspect, it would appear, of his combat military duties. The Prosecution must prove, therefore, in each case that Stanisic, not the likes of Simovic, were passing these types of orders. It is equally wholly unsatisfactory to take undisputed evidence of Badza's role and command over Kojic prior to Trnovo and presume, nonetheless, that Kojic must have been acting at the behest of Stanisic. Why? Because he was employed in the DB. Mr. Martin is under my control during this Court hearing but if he fails to comport himself unprofessionally during his ICTR case, why should I take the blame? If we can turn to slide 12, please. The fourth strategy which reduces or risks reducing the burden of proof is the Prosecution's attempt to obscure the distinction between institutions and individuals. Of particular concern is the Prosecution's attempt to link Stanisic to every single action of any individual with any DB connection, from Bogdanovic's superior to Simatovic to Badza and so on, without evidence that they're acting at Stanisic's behest. The Prosecution need to isolate what are the acts of the JCE members, what and who -- sorry. Who are their tools distinct from Stanisic's contribution and his tools and assist Your Honours in a question of whether, in the end, Stanisic's contribution, if found, was significant. Slides 13, 14, and 15 are illustrations from the Prosecution's final brief of this dangerous attempt to collectivise responsibility. Slide 15 is a particularly -- if we can turn to that, please -- is a particularly cogent -- it's confidential, sorry, not to be shown to the public. Slide 15 is a particularly cogent example of the third and the fourth strategy combined. The Prosecution invites you to attribute Milos arms supplies on behalf of the Serbian MUP to Stanisic on no other basis than the DB used him since 1991 to gather intelligence, from intelligence to arms supplies, from the MUP to Stanisic and the Serbian DB in a cutting and pasting and conflating exercise that has no place in a criminal trial. Finally, if we can turn to slide 16 perhaps most seriously, the Prosecution have approached the evidence in the ways listed on this slide and more, we say, strategies to fill the gaps where evidence should be, to lead the Chamber down the wrong evidential path. We accept as noted by the Prosecution yesterday one mistake in our final brief at paragraph 1175. We accept that the Skorpions only became part of the reserve forces of the SAJ in 1998 or 1999. That error and perhaps there's a handful of more, we suspect not many, are dwarfed by the Prosecution's errors. And slide 16 is an outline of some of the most serious. What does this mean? Well, we say this: That the only way to put a coherent case against Mr. Stanisic together is to approach this evidence selectively and engage in selective submissions, perhaps then, the evidence might look reliable. Unsubstantiated allegations unreasonable inferences, selective quoting of evidence that includes failing to bring to Your Honours' attention their own witness' retractions on critical issues, reliance on evidence that needs corroboration, using evidence admitted and argued for admission for one purpose for another, and so on. Slides 17 through 29 are some representative samples taken from the Prosecution final brief, demonstrating this unfortunate approach. Seventeen, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, and 27 are confidential. I will not take Your Honours through them but leave them with Your Honours for consideration later. Forceful advocacy is one thing. Ignoring retractions is quite another. Relying heavily on Mladic's notebook to prove that Stanisic agreed with the goals of the JCE or that he was engaged in supplies of weapons without acknowledging that Mladic is an accomplice, that he has removed Srebrenica from his notebook along with Sarajevo, not acknowledging that there is it evidence to show that he was part of a VRS military security plan to declare all associates of MUP Serbia as extremists and paramilitaries is a curious approach to a fair trial. Why, may we ask, does the Prosecution suggest that Kovacevic's evidence concerning Trnovo should be corroborated but not that of Mladic, as they said yesterday at transcript 20239? Well, the reason is obvious. Kovacevic isn't important for this trial. Mladic, given the paucity of evidence elsewhere, may well be. The Prosecution claimed yesterday that the Stanisic Defence fails to explain how implicating Stanisic and sending Arkan's Men and the Skorpions to Pauk would benefit Mladic. They are right. We didn't explain that. We thought it was obvious. It's the same answer to the question: Why are Srebrenica and Sarajevo not mentioned in his notebooks. It's the same answer to the question: Why are the Prosecution using that evidence to draw massive inferences with regard to Stanisic's command, or alleged command, of these units from 1991 to 1995. Let me pose, if I may, two questions for the Prosecution in regard to these notebooks and this particular attempt to implicate Stanisic in the Skorpions and Arkan. Milovanovic claimed, and we heard this yesterday, that Stanisic was more knowledgeable than him in relation to some things in the Podrinje. Putting aside the fact that it was the time of the Oric's attacks so, of course, the chief of state security made it his business to know what was going on there. Milovanovic, effectively conceded that he knew more than Stanisic in relation to most things. We can safely assume that Mladic was equally well-informed. As we discuss at paragraphs 138 to 143 and 185 to 1090 of our closing brief, the Skorpions had been part of an ongoing rotation of 11th Corps units assisting the VRS and Fikret Abdic during 1994 before Pauk and continuing into Pauk. So why would Stanisic go to a meeting and tell Mladic what Mladic undoubtedly knew to be true? That the Skorpions had gone to Pauk but in fact they were part of a 11th Corps rotation. Or let me put it differently: Why would Stanisic go to a meeting and tell Mladic what he knew not to be true? Stanisic saying, I sent the Skorpions, when Mladic must have known this was the 11th Corps. Secondly, why would Stanisic tell Mladic that he had sent men from Erdut, meaning Arkan men, when according to the Prosecution case Simatovic arranged to collect Arkan's Men from Belgrade. Stanisic, the astoundingly well-informed DB chief must have known what almost everyone else knew: That Arkan's camp in Erdut closed in late 1993 and only reopened in May of 1995. Your Honours will find our arguments developed in paragraph 1040 of our closing brief. Arkan's Men were not at Erdut. This is a clumsy attempt by Mladic to implicate Stanisic and even if it's not, we suggest the right approach is to look for corroboration and the Prosecution's attempt to rely upon these notebooks without, is likely to create the conditions for a mischarge of justice. If we can turn to slide 30, please. Not to be shown to the public. We submit that the Prosecution of this case has forgotten to approach the case with the degree of solemnity required before asking for a life sentence. It maintains the obvious myth, we say, that they have adduced evidence to show that Stanisic commanded and supplied Arkan's Men since 1991. There isn't the evidence. And what did the Prosecution do? Your Honours can see what they have done in slide 30. Slide 31 and 32 and 33 also show the attempt to conflate evidence that relates to Arkan in 1994 and 1995 and make it appear that it relates to 1991, 1992, and 1993. So to conclude part 1 of these closing remarks, the reality is, these strategies would not be needed if the case against Mr. Stanisic wasn't so weak. It cannot sustain the weight of the allegations. As part 2 of this speech will further examine, it cannot even start to establish that he was Milosevic's right-hand man or otherwise a co-ordinator of the political or military activity. That's the originating premise of this trial. The evidence doesn't establish that he was the paramount co-ordinator of supplies. It doesn't even establish that he was a supplier from Belgrade. We say it does not establish that he controlled a single paramilitary force. When viewed fairly and when the law is properly applied, the Prosecution case establishes nothing that we did not know. Stanisic was proximate to the events. The burden and standard of proof is not some ethereal concept that cannot be defined for practical purposes. The Prosecution's avoidance of inconvenient evidence and the spinning of much of the rest is the antithesis of that standard. Which requires first a consideration of the totality of the evidence, and second, the exclusion of all reasonable inferences. Mr. Stanisic's legitimate tasks involve proximity to the event. Suspicion arises. Nothing more has been shown. If I can turn to the second part of the speech. If we can turn to slide 34. We want to spend a little time contextualising the case presented in the Prosecution brief. With regard to Mr. Stanisic's alleged role as a channel of communication or facilitator of the JCE, as can be seen at paragraph 187 of the Prosecution closing brief, the Prosecution's case is that Mr. Stanisic served as a channel of communication facilitating the JCE members in furtherance of crimes pursuant to the common purpose. He is said to have co-ordinated the activities between Milosevic and Babic, Milosevic and Hadzic, Milosevic and Martic, Milosevic and Karadzic. Mr. Stanisic was not a military commander or a political leader. He did not command the armies or sit in the Supreme Defence council of the FRY making political decisions. The expansive role alleged formation, financing, supply of arms and equipment in the RSK, the SBWS, and Bosnia, the use and control of special units is premised on him co-ordinating and facilitating the activities of the political leadership. Second part of this closing will examine this premise with regard to each of the crime bases and each of the principle leaders. The Prosecution's case, we submit, has not been proven. With regard to the SAO Krajina, Your Honours will appreciate that the case against Mr. Stanisic is premised on his alleged relationship with Martic and Babic. This enabled Mr. Stanisic, so the theory goes, to control the military, the paramilitaries, Golubic, the Knindzas, as well as a special unit Arkan and the Skorpions. We will address first Martic and then Babic. Slide 35 should be confidential, please. Slide 35 sums up the Prosecution's principle allegations concerning Mr. Stanisic's alleged role as co-ordinator of Martic's activities. If Your Honours have a look, very briefly Your Honours will see that the most startling feature of this critical aspect of the case is the almost exclusive reliance on JF-039, one of Martic's hired men. Technically corroboration is not required, but, of course, if Your Honours, we submit, are to respect the presumption of innocence, it is essential in this instances because to establish that Stanisic was the key co-ordinator of all Martic's activities, common sense and legal principle dictates that more than one man's word is required, especially JF-039 an accomplice and a man with a reputation as a bully and a thief. Your Honours will recall, JF-039's account. We discuss him at length in our closing brief. His account is replete with contradictions on vital issues. The Prosecution may well respond and say, Well, no, his evidence is corroborated by Babic. As we know, Babic claimed in -- that the relationship between Martic and Stanisic overwhelmed him and let him into a violation of international law. JF-039 was relied upon to provide the detail of this alleged relationship, claiming that he observed Mr. Stanisic co-ordinating all the assistance from the Milosevic government to Martic's nascent police force, there can be little doubt, we submit, that both men perjured themselves. If we can turn to slide 36, which should be confidential, please. I hope Your Honours have the book of slides also, because what we should do, I'd invite Your Honours to do - yes, thank you - is to look at 36 and 37 together. Both Babic and JF-039 contradict each other in the most fundamental manner, demonstrating that the case against Stanisic from the outset, like a house built on sand, lacks any real foundation. In sum, both Babic and JF-039 claimed separately to have participated in the arrangements that led to Milosevic's assistance to Martic's police and the creation and supply of Golubic. JF-039 claims that the arrangements for creating and supplying the police and creating Golubic were made in January of 1991 in a meeting between Bogdanovic, Stanisic, and Martic. It should be noted that this was allegedly the second stage, according to JF-039, of the, let's call it, the Golubic plan, a plan to create paramilitary forces that had already commenced, according to JF-039, in September of 1990. Babic, on the other hand, claims that the arrangements were first made in March of 1991 and Golubic was not part of those plans. He was, in fact, surprised when men from the DB turned up to create Golubic. So the Prosecution ask you to accept that Babic, completely unaware of Martic's arrangements with Milosevic and Stanisic, which had begun in September of 1990, went along to see Milosevic in March, on the 20th of March, 1991, seeking assistance for the Ministry of Interior's nascent police force. So according to JF-039's account, at the time when Babic went seeking for help for the SAO Krajina's new police force, Stanisic had already been facilitating seven months of supplies. And since January of 1991, three months before, Stanisic had been delivering weapons in MUP trucks with blue registration plates, indicating they were from the Serbian police, driven by men wearing special police uniforms, straight into the heart of Knin. I think we can agree that we would need some dark shadows to hide those trucks, and yet no one, not the authorities in Bosnia as these trucks travelled through, not Babic, no one but JF-039 appears to have noticed. A case of the left hand not knowing what the right hand was doing, or is somebody, or both JF-039 or Babic, being economical with the truth? Is it possible that -- or likely that Babic went separately to Milosevic in March of 1991, seeking urgent help for the police, completely unaware that Stanisic was co-ordinating Milosevic's supplies to Martic and had been doing so since September of 1990? Could we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think it is also maybe the time for the break, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on whether we split up in two portions of -- we had a bit of a late start. So if you go on for seven or eight minutes then we would have equal division between the two portions. But if Mr. Stanisic would prefer to have a break now then we'll take that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No I think we can continue. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we continue for another seven to eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So let's suspend common sense for a moment and presume that Babic was completely unaware and he did go to Milosevic in March of 1991 without appreciating that Stanisic on behalf of Milosevic had been co-ordinating for seven months. If we can turn to slide 37. Not to be shown to the -- oh, I think it can be shown to the public. Apologies. As Your Honours will see from slide 37, following the meeting in March of 1991, Babic spoke to Martic's assistant in the police, Zelenbaba. Did Zelenbaba turn around to Babic and say, Dear president, let me tell you a story about Martic's brother, Mr. Stanisic, who we trust 100 per cent, don't you know he's been delivering weapons for seven months. You didn't know that? No. As an aside, why did Milosevic, Bogdanovic, or Stanisic not tell Babic as his March 1991 meeting, Stop wasting our time, Mr. Babic. We have been assisting you for seven months. Not just to create the police but for the barricades, the nightguards, we're setting up a great training base. Nobody said that to Babic. And what does Zelenbaba tell Babic when Babic approaches him? Zelenbaba, Martic's assistant says, it is Kertes who has been kicking open the doors of the TO. Nothing about MUP trucks. Nothing about Stanisic. Nothing about this so-called brotherly love. Could we turn to slide 38, please, because there's a third version. It's confidential. According to the Prosecution thesis, P975 is an excerpt from a speech Milosevic gave when addressing members of local councils on the 16th of March, 1991. Allegedly it is a reiteration of an order the day before that led to the creation of Golubic. Slide 38 contains the relevant excerpt. And yet, according to JF-039, upon which the case against Stanisic hangs, in relation to supplies and co-ordination with Martic, Milosevic had been engaged in creating new police forces in Krajina since September of 1990. Or at least from January 1991. In January 1991, according to JF-039, Stanisic had effectively acted on Milosevic's order for Golubic to open in a very short time. And yet not even Milosevic appears to have know about his own co-ordinating of supplies or his own decision to create Golubic two months before. Doesn't make sense and it never will. JF-039 built the house on sand and Babic and Milosevic knocked it down. Slide 39, please. It should remain public -- confidential. JF-039's evidence is absurd and demonstrably so. JF-039 perjured himself. Slide 39 contains dispositive proof of his failure to remain consistent on the most basic of issues. Did Stanisic's arming or his co-ordinating on behalf of Milosevic stop in June, or did it go on for the entire five years? Let us examine a bit further. I don't know if this is a convenient time. I was going to move to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at 75 minutes, approximately so. Let's take the break now. Then you have another session of 75 minutes after the break, and then the Simatovic Defence can start after that. We resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Let us examine further, JF-039's tale of Stanisic's intimate relation with Martic and Stanisic's role as the channel of communication with Milosevic. Apparently that relationship was so intimate and affectionate that Martic often referred to Stanisic as "my brother" and he said he trusted him 100 per cent. And, yet, according to JF-039, and discussed in our brief at paragraphs 302 to 320 particularly, in June 1991, Martic, threw Simatovic out of Knin in order to seize full control over his police and TO. As I've mentioned, according to JF-039, Stanisic's supplies of weapons stopped, what, according to one version of JF-039's account Stanisic supplies of weapons stopped in May or June of 1991. As discussed in our closing brief at paragraph 78, in early March of 1992, Martic ordered Rajic, Simatovic, Starcevic and Orlovic to be arrested because, and I quote, "these men all worked directly for Simatovic and were members of the Serbian DB." JF-039 claimed at T-7282 that Martic attempted to arrest these men effectively dissolving the Krajina DB because he believed that Orlovic was passing information more to Stanisic than to him. JF-031 offered some corroboration of that account, noting that Martic's principal grievance was that he never received correct information. Your Honours will find that at paragraph 79 of our brief. Draca at transcript 16778 confirmed that Martic had an ongoing dispute with Stanisic and the Serbian DB. It was only in January 1993 that very limited contact was re-established between the RSK DB and the Serbian DB. If we could to slide 40 to finish this chronology. As we discuss at paragraph 1118 of our brief, on the 4th of the October, 1994, Martic accused Stanisic of using Kostic and Kojic to undermine his authority, including kidnapping his minister of the interior, Prilic -- or Prijic in August of 1994 and detaining Martic himself on the border crossing. Slide 40 contains part of a phone call Martic made to Milosevic. As we can see, Martic was refusing to meet Stanisic in 1994, claiming that Stanisic is: "Tripping me at every step and causes trouble. This is really below any level." So as this brief chronology shows, from June 1991, according to JF-039 himself, Martic attempted to remove the Serbian DB's alleged influence from the Krajina. And yet, despite this clear evidence of Martic's relatively consistent paranoia that Stanisic and the Serbian DB were undermining his authority, Your Honours are supposed to conclude that Martic regarded Stanisic as his brother and trusted him 100 per cent. That is not to argue that Stanisic was never in contact with Martic. That would be preposterous. It was would be as unrealistic as a proposition that any contact or assistance to the RSK must have been in furtherance of crime. It would have been negligent to decline to form any relation with Martic given the implications of Martic's clumsy leadership for the security of Serbia. At paragraph 669 of the Prosecution's closing brief, the Prosecution claims that Milosevic's own words confirm Stanisic's role as a liaison between himself and Martic. They claim that: "In one intercepted conversation in September 1991, regarding a protocol for a cease-fire in the SAO Krajina, Milosevic said to Karadzic, So, I told you of it, sir, as he was this contact with Milan, to say that Martic should sign this technical protocol." Unfortunately, the Prosecution's position declines to distinguish conduct in furtherance of crime and contact with the leadership of the RSK to advance peace. Being tasked by Milosevic to have Martic signed a European Union-sponsored peace proposal is one thing, co-ordinating supplies to further crimes, quite another. As will be outlined in the remainder of this closing, Stanisic's role with regard to such peace initiatives is well documented. To this extent, it might be considered a channel of communication. His contact with Martic to urge him to sign an agreement, or protocol, as a step towards peace was the first of many other attempts to further peace initiatives from the Wynaendts Peace Conference, to Vance, to Dayton and beyond, we say this evidence is in disputable and stands in marked contrast to the thrust of the Prosecution case. If we could turn to slide 41, please. The Prosecution falls into the same error with regard to Stanisic's role assisting with implementing the Vance Plan. At paragraphs 82 to 84 of the Prosecution final brief, the Prosecution assert that P686, an intercepted conversation between Karadzic and Stanisic, dated the 7th of January, 1992, shows that: "Stanisic played an integral role in -- in the shaping of the soon-to-be RSK's government concept, making government appointments, planning military police activities in SBWS, and consolidating Serbian territories outside of Serbia." This slide contains the relevant part of that conversation. Despite the Prosecution attempt to extrapolate from that conversation, a cursory examination of this intercept shows Karadzic and Stanisic were talking about the difficulties of having the Vance Plan implemented, nothing to do, stretches one might, with forcible removal of Croats from Croatia. The fact that the Prosecution relies upon it is an eloquent illustration of the frailty of their case. This conversation and others we will see in a moment stands as a rebuttal of the role Stanisic is alleged to have played. It is a illustration of his lack of criminal intent. If we could go to the next slide, please. Actually, before we do, Your Honours will see Stanisic in the 7th of January, 1992, expressing his frustration with the lack of political activity there, the RSK, we can agree with the Prosecution on that, as he says: "Because all these people are complete incompetent jerks and immature as well ... I had trouble explaining them to be patient and to get serious and get to work." Stanisic notes he met 44 commanders to explain the situation and notes that discontent that exists there. The same conversation. Stanisic is, we suggest, pulling his hair out with frustration. He refers to the leadership of the RSK as fierce Chetniks: "There are a lot of radical people there who are angry at the entire world. They are sitting in these border areas for a year and are fighting. Do you understand." Stanisic says he's going to make a round on the field and make some -- some kind of concept. The idea that this intercept stands as proof as Stanisic's war-like activities or his integral role in the shaping of the RSK's government's concept as the furtherance of a criminal purpose is a fanciful proposition. He was doing his level best to engineer a concept that would reduce the discontents of those war commanders, who, rather than implementing Vance or moving towards peace, had other ideas. Does this name-calling from Stanisic, his obvious frustration, sound like a man who had played the critical role co-ordinating their activities and their crimes, or someone who admired their work, or someone who had a vested interest in their war-like activities, or shared, more importantly, any criminal intent? Can we turn to slide 43, please. The Prosecution's unreasonable approach to Stanisic's alleged role as the facilitator of the JCE is even more apparent with regard to Babic. This is dealt with at paragraphs 20, 669 to 671 of the Prosecution brief. Slide 43 sums up the claimed support for this alleged role. Let us examine this proposition that the Prosecution claims stands as its dispositive proof of Stanisic's contribution to the JCE. It is a stark illustration of the dangerous ruse at the heart of the Prosecution case. As Your Honours will discover through an examination of footnotes 2324 to 2326, the Prosecution brief, entitled: Channel of communication, there is not a single piece of evidence to suggest that Stanisic facilitated Babic's contact with Milosevic, let alone shared his extremist views. How that allegation sits with the parallel structure thesis is yet to be explained. On the contrary, there can be little doubt that Stanisic regarded him quite accurately on one view, even though it's not nice to speak ill of the dead, as one of the radical incompetent and immature jerks of the RSK leadership that stood in the way of the Vance Plan. The Prosecution provides one example of Stanisic's alleged co-ordinating role with Babic. If we could turn to slide 44, please. The example is that Stanisic facilitated the Vance Plan. Slide 44, 45, 46, and 47, reflect excerpts of P683, P686, 87, and P690, all conversations between Karadzic and Stanisic in January of 1992. Because the Prosecution declined to distinguish conduct in furtherance of crime from other conduct they claim that these conversations support their case. On the contrary, we urge Your Honours to examine these intercepts. They offer a window into Mr. Stanisic's mind, his contemporaneous repudiation of Babic's radical attitude and his attempts to have the Vance Plan implemented, a plan that offered the only prospect that Croats might be able to return home. As slide 44 shows, on the 5th of January, 1992, Stanisic explains how he has tried without success to tie Babic down. Karadzic notes that he could spoil things, meaning, obviously, the Vance Plan. In slide 45 - we can turn to that - the men can be seen - Karadzic and Stanisic - from the 7th of January continuing that theme. Karadzic in characteristically colourful language suggests that the army should grab Babic by the balls to force him to sign the Vance Plan. Your Honours will note that it is Karadzic, not Stanisic, who acts as the peace-maker between Babic and Martic. Stanisic notes that Babic's "radical attitude towards everybody can finish really bad." Turn to slide 46, please. Your Honours, if one looks at slide 46, 47, 48 and 49, these are excerpts from the conversations on the 12th and the 22nd of January, 1992. Slide 46 has Karadzic informing Stanisic that he mad a plan with Babic to go see Milosevic. It's noteworthy that he has to inform Stanisic of that fact. If Stanisic was the facilitator between Babic and Milosevic, surely he would have made that arrangement, not Karadzic. Both men agree that a favourable ending is only a step away. Stanisic expresses his fear there will be a total war. That's what he is afraid of. In slide 42, both men agree that their conversation mens nothing. They have to tell those that disagree with them. They make a plan to act. They make a plan to meet and act. Stanisic notes that he does not want to be shown as part of the initiative. Slide 48 contains exerts from Exhibit P690, a conversation the two men had on the 22nd of January, 1992. Karadzic and Stanisic discuss the way forward and how Karadzic has negotiated with Babic to come to a comprise, to allow the Krajina to express some reservations with the Vance Plan. Stanisic notes his relief. Stanisic -- sorry. Slide 49 contains the only remark in this whole case, spanning more than five years of ethnic conflict, that provides an iota of evidence to support a suggestion that Stanisic might have harboured ill-feelings to the Croat population. It is worthwhile examining this conversation in context and in the context of the frustration that both men have clearly shown with Babic and the RSK leadership. Karadzic notes an undesirability of war continue in the RSK, stating that: "Nobody will win. We will all be impoverished and ruined." He notes that without Tudjman and the Croatian Serbs showing some elasticity and goodwill they will be in for 30 years of torture. Stanisic concurs, noting that they must push them all to Belgrade. He notes with obvious frustration: "There is nothing left for us to do or we'll exterminate them completely, so let's see where we end up. If they want it, then they'll have a all-out war, better to do it like decent people." The proposition that a single remark can stand as any evidence of Stanisic's criminal intent is a distortion of the remark and the context of the conversation. There is not a single person in this room who has not uttered in frustration an inflammatory remark or an overly aggressive comment that they regretted immediately. Stanisic was obviously frustrated at the incompetence and reckless behaviour of both Babic and Tudjman. That the Prosecution is only able to offer this one remark throughout the whole of the indictment period is a cogent illustration of Mr. Stanisic's coolness under fire, his racial tolerance in the midst of a hateful conflict and the falseness of this indictments. He knew there was no choice: Sign the peace agreement like decent people rather than continuing the war. He was tasked to help persuade the RSK leadership to sign the peace agreement. If that makes him a channel of communication, then so be it. If we can turn to slide 50. Let us examine very briefly Stanisic's alleged role as co-ordinator of Hadzic's activities. Prosecution claim that Stanisic co-ordinated the SBWS, including the special units, the Red Berets, Arkan, the Skorpions, et cetera, through his co-ordinating relationship with Hadzic. Slide 50 contains the Prosecution's principal allegations. These allegations are almost wholly unsubstantiated, at best supported by patently unreliable hearsay. I have already outlined our position with regards to points 5 and 6 on the slides in front of you. I will not return to this obvious reversal of the burden of standard of proof. Slide 51 contains the single piece of evidentiary lied on in support of the allegation that Hadzic viewed Stanisic as the link between Milosevic and Badza by stating that Hadzic told him this, but he can't say anything more than that. The witness Bogunovic fairly conceded the limited value of his own evidence, a reasonable position to take with regard to this evidence and Hadzic and the breadth of the allegation sought to be established by this evidence. There is no reliable evidence that Badza was ever denied access to Milosevic. As we discuss in our final brief, Badza's subsequent and meteoric rise from SI commander to deputy minister of the interior shows his closeness to the SPS party stalwart Sokolovic, who was minister of interior, which in turn stands as cogent evidence of a relationship with Milosevic. As slide 52 shows - if we can turn to that - the Prosecution also alleges that Hadzic implemented recommendations and orders from Belgrade after meeting with Milosevic and Stanisic. Despite an impressively large footnote most of the evidence relied upon in support of that concerns Milosevic, not Stanisic. The evidence that places Stanisic at these meetings is limited to two witnesses. The irrepressible Mr. Babic, never one to pass up an opportunity for fabrication or exaggeration, and Mr. Bogunovic. As slide 52 shows, both make assertions devoid of any of the type of detail that might turn an allegation into something concrete, let alone satisfy Your Honours of the truth beyond a reasonable doubt. It is impossible to be satisfied that Stanisic was present at the meetings. Even if he was present at the meetings, the Prosecution has adduced no evidence that could satisfy this Chamber that he was instructing or advising Hadzic. Your Honours will not be able to identify a single instruction or a piece of advice conveyed by Stanisic. Regarding Babic's evidence, let us apply the burden and standard of proof and recall Babic's evidence must be corroborated. It has not been and should be disregarded. Slide 53, if we can turn to that, contains some excerpts from Bogunovic's evidence in relation to meetings he had with Stanisic. This has been ignored by the Prosecution. Bogunovic was the minister of the interior for the SBWS. If Stanisic was engaged in passing on Milosevic's instructions it is logical to presume that he would not limit this to instructions straight to Hadzic. Indeed, the implication of the Prosecution case is that it extended to the whole of the SBWS government from Kojic to Mrgud, and so on. And, yet, on the rare occasion Bogunovic met Stanisic, as we discuss in the SBWS section of our brief, Stanisic did not speak. He sat and took notes. As we discuss in paragraph 432 of our closing brief this is precisely what the evidence shows he did when he met the minister of defence during the five meetings he had from 1991 to 1995. These meetings concerned updates on political events, refugees, and once again the implementation of the Vance Plan. Silence and taking notes is curious behaviour for a man whose principal task was to pass instructions from Milosevic to the SBWS government. Passing information to Milosevic on these types of security-related subjects is one thing, passing instructions and orders in furtherance of crime, something quite different. Slide 53 sums up some of Bogunovic's evidence that is relevant to that submission. Slide 54 the Prosecution wants Your Honours to accept Stanisic was the link between Milosevic and Arkan and Badza for whom Milosevic exerted influence over Hadzic on the ground. Slide 53 contains the evidence relied upon. The Prosecution should think twice before accusing a man who had been linked with Arkan and really needs to be based on more than a witness's assumption. Finally, the Prosecution allege that in the capacity of facilitator Stanisic arrived Dalj in mid-September of 1991, expressing outrage that Vukovar had not yet fallen to the Serbs, demanded a meeting with Hadzic, a meeting which would further the common purpose with respect to Vukovar. During the meeting, Stanisic, it is it alleged, planned operations to liberate Vukovar as soon as possible. Let us analyse that for a moment. No longer working in the shadows but bellowing in public like a market trader selling his wears. If the Prosecution were interested in contextualization they would not have relied upon this allegation. No witness but JF-032 heard Stanisic, or heard of Stanisic turning up in Dalj and screaming. Bogunovic, according to the witness at T-4757, was supposed to be present at the screaming. JF-029 was, according to JF-032 at transcript 4759, supposed to have been present at the planned meeting. At transcript 6044, Bogunovic confirmed he never heard of such an event. Neither Bogunovic, the minister of the interior or JF-029 offered a scintilla of evidence to corroborate this fabricated, largely hearsay tale. As critically, there is not a single piece of other evidence to suggest that Stanisic was involved with planning the Vukovar operations. One would have thought that at least one insider in this trial or any other trial would have learnt such a role. The Prosecution seeks to persuade you that a professional counter-intelligence officer and Hadzic, a warehouse manager by trade, sat down and helped to plan the biggest military operation of that time. Oddly, nobody but JF-032, from the leadership of the SBWS to those in the JNA appear to have noticed such an important contribution to one of the biggest crimes in this terrible war. Of course, it's a lie. Could we turn to slide 55, please. Finally we turn to the Prosecution's originating premise concerning Bosnia. As with the Croatian crime bases, their case rests on Stanisic being a channel of communication. Or, as they put it at paragraph 675 and 676: "A gate-keeper and liaison between Milosevic and Karadzic which parallels Stanisic's role vis-a-vis Martic, Babic, and Hadzic." This originating premise is a critical part of the Prosecution case. It cannot sensibly be suggested that Stanisic had any real relationship with Mladic. As the Mladic notebooks made clear, Stanisic was only introduced to him in July 1993. Mladic, as I have said, did not have Stanisic's number until July 1995. Milovanovic thought Stanisic was a waiter in early 1993. So Stanisic cannot have been co-ordinating through that military line. He must have been through the political line. This political relationship allegedly allowed him to parachute Arkan's Men and the Skorpions at will into the VRS zone of responsibility. No doubt, Mladic will claim it had nothing to do with him. As we can see from slide 55, the Prosecution makes various allegations concerning Stanisic's relationship with Karadzic. The most startling feature of these expansive claims is the evidence lied upon to establish Stanisic's role during the five-year indictment period, his evidence that comes from intercepts from July 1991 until January 1992, and a diary that places Stanisic on the 6th of September, 1991, at a meeting with Bogdanovic, who is clearly acting as a contact man for Jovic involved, we would say, in limited supply to vulnerable Serbian villages in Bosnia. Even if the Prosecution's interpretation of these intercepts does disclose that Stanisic was at the time co-ordinating Milosevic's supply of weapons or his political project, the interference the Prosecution urges is astonishing. Despite a whole military campaign the creation of new political structures, the transformation of the JNA into the VRS, and a myriad of other criminal and non-criminal events, the Prosecution suggests that you can be satisfied Stanisic maintained this relationship through the indictment period, an ambitious inference, indeed, not because they can point to circumstantial evidence of that relationship continuing, oral testimony, documentary evidence such as assembly minutes, Karadzic's diary which was on the 65 ter list, the Mladic notebooks, intelligence reports, or even the usual multiple hearsay evidence that is a regrettable feature of this case, but because of a handful of conversations before the war. Slides 56 and 57 contain a selection of the adjudicated facts in this case. They place the Bosnian Serbs' movement to war in some chronological context. Even if Stanisic was given carte blanche by Milosevic to supply Bosnian Serb villages with weapons in late 1991, or facilitated the political events until January 1992, it is difficult, we submit, to see how this could have been linked to this criminal purpose. In the words of the Prosecution's requested Third Adjudicated Fact, number 97, it was only during 1992 when the SDS started contemplating military conflict as a likelihood and no longer as a mere possibility. Calls to take over territory became "strong and distinct only at the beginning of January 1992." At paragraphs 88 to 117, the Prosecution discuss these intercepted conversations under the title: "Implementation of the JCE in Bosnia." It includes -- or they include various accusations including Karadzic's and Stanisic's alleged belligerence suggesting that neither man was seriously interested in peace. We submit that these allegation, even if taken at face value and accurate, have little to do with this trial. But on the contrary, the allegations made by the Prosecution and the provocative title: "Implementation of the JCE in Bosnia," are designed to persuade Your Honours that a criminal purpose began in Bosnia the same time as the one in Croatia and for one reason only. The best evidence of Mr. Stanisic's involvement with Karadzic began at that time and ended in January of 1992. Moreover, this evidence does not even begin to prove that Stanisic was not interested in peace, let alone that he was pursuing crime. A reasonable interpretation of the relevant intercepts show precisely the reverse. First of all, the very premise of the Prosecution's allegations are dubious to say the least. Your Honours are invited to believe that even though Stanisic was doing his best to tie Babic down, speak to 44 discontented commanders and deal with the Chetniks of the RSK, simultaneously he was determined to pursue war in Bosnia. Why would a man who has castigated the RSK leadership betray such a lack of logic? In order to reinterpret the intercepts, the Prosecution cut and paste events, people, and motivations to prove a point that has no basis in the evidence. If Your Honours have the Prosecution's closing brief, if you would turn to paragraphs 94 to 95 of the Prosecution brief, here, the Prosecution cut and paste from Karadzic's comments in August 1991 to the effect that the Bosnian Serbs should do everything that Brdjanin is thinking; and then suggests that Karadzic's comments are chilling in light of extreme views that Brdjanin held in 1992 where he advocated forcible transfer; and nice photograph at paragraph 95 of Stanisic and Simatovic, the latter wearing a military uniform, indisputably from much later than this time, standing next to Karadzic nicely completes the exercise in unfair assertion. At paragraph 96 of the Prosecution closing, they take Stanisic's role in attempting to prevent war and spin it to suggest the reverse. The Prosecution claims that Stanisic's involvement with Brdjanin demonstrates his authority in Bosnia by August 1991. As I've said, of course, even if that was true it might not be true at a time when the political and military events have been transformed and the calls to take over territory had become more distinct. It was quite possible to have influence in August 1991 and little in 1992. In fact the burden of proof, we submit, demands that Your Honours presume precisely that, until proven otherwise. Moreover it is, of course, possible to use influence for good even if crimes were on the rise. An examination of the intercepts and the role that Stanisic appears to have played shows precisely that. Slide 58 shows the role that Stanisic played at that time. Similar to his efforts in Croatia he kept his head when all around was losing theirs. He took Brdjanin fishing to calm him down and prevent him from doing anything stupid so that the Bosnian Serbs would say not derail the negotiations. Alija would then have to tell the Muslims why they wanted to wage war against the Serbs, as stated by Karadzic. He, Alija, would have to explain it. We submit that the reality appears to be that Stanisic, in 1991 was regarded as a man who might play a role in calming the excesses of others, preventing war and advancing towards peace. His role appears to be extended to Bosnia, as well as Croatia. It was a role he played later with regard to Dayton and a myriad of other activities that we say helped to bring peace and stability to the region. Try as they might to interpret Stanisic's role alternatively or cast dispersions on his motives there is a consistent line in these intercepts of Stanisic playing a positive role. This is it further demonstrated in a conversation between Karadzic and Milosevic on the 8th of October, 1991. Slide 59 and 60 are excerpts from that conversation. We return to the RSK. Milosevic notes that the RSK leadership will not even turn up for the peace conference negotiations. He notes that one man, probably Babic, thinks that everyone should get down on their knees when he shows up. Both men seem to agree that Stanisic should be asked to get involved to find a way to get the leadership to turn up to the peace conference. They agree that Stanisic should invite ten of the smart ones from the opposition to come to a meeting to find a way forward. Once again, the Prosecution declines to draw distinctions between actions in furtherance of peace and actions in furtherance of crime. Prosecution at paragraph 679 of their brief claims that this conversation is an illustration of the integral role played by Stanisic in the relationship between Karadzic and Milosevic. As we discuss in our closing brief, the State Security Service was not built for war, nor did Stanisic have those skills. There were plenty of men who could prosecutes the war and very few had the political nuance and the diplomatic skills to keep a cool head. When the war suited Milosevic or Karadzic's aims, others from Perisic to Mladic, to Arkan to Badza, were required. When a cool hand on the tiller was required, it appears, Stanisic, a man schooled in counter-intelligence, a perfect training for diplomacy perhaps could play a role. If we are to extrapolate from these 1991 and earlier 1992 intercepts to make large claims concerning their significance throughout the indictment period, let us extrapolate from a reasonable interpretation of the conversations. Having influence and authority is not an indication of criminal intent. And so move to section 3 of our speech and our concluding remarks, the evidence that Stanisic was number two to Milosevic, or more importantly, that he played a co-ordinating role in the war is devoid of evidential support. If we're right about this then alongside the collapse of the 28 elite trainer thesis what is left? As we've outlined in detail, in order to compensate for the lack of evidence, the Prosecution have attempted to build a new case through ignoring the strictures of JCE law and urging unreasonable inferences based on a partial view of the evidence. This will not assist the ascertainment of the truth. The careful distinctions that need to be drawn to find the truth and to ensure that justice is done are not to be found in the Prosecution's final brief. It is transparently a highlight of the most incriminatory aspect of the evidence untroubled by reflections on reliability or credibility. It incorporates an attempt to rebuild the house using new sands, whilst insisting that the sand has a significant relationship to something more substantial. The reality is that the Prosecution thesis is unrealistic. They, not the Defence, are running from the evidence. We confront the evidence in our final brief, and we offer reasonable explanations, a practical demonstration of the approach that must be taken to the burden and standard of proof. If I, with the greatest of respect, can offer the type of analysis that Mr. Stanisic's case deserves and which the Prosecution case seeks to avoid, by referring you to slide 61, and allegation 6. In attempt to link Stanisic to Dragan, the Prosecution relies upon P671, an intercepted conversation from the 29th of November, 1991, that they claim, at paragraph 99 of their final brief, demonstrates that Stanisic intended to engage Captain Dragan and Simatovic to assist Karadzic in the way that they'd already assisted Martic. It's a forgery. It's obvious. Slide 61 contains the salient parts of this purportedly authenticate intercept. It is the only intercept, we dispute, it is the only intercept out of 97 produced by a witness that has no corresponding audiotape to verify its authenticity. That, of course, creates some doubt concerning its authenticity. That makes it especially important to look at it in context. First, as we discuss at paragraph 1036 of our closing brief, there is it evidence that the Bosnian Serb leadership from at least mid-1994 adopted a policy of blaming the Serbian MUP, characterising them as extremists, paramilitaries and destroying incriminatory documents. That makes a forgery a bit more likely. Have the Prosecution removed that doubt through providing corroborative support? The Prosecution has not produced a single piece of evidence to corroborate this so-called intercept and its claim that in November 1991 Stanisic was commanding Dragan and Simatovic on military operations in the RSK. We suggest there is not even a single piece of evidence to suggest that Stanisic commanded Dragan or directed him in war operations, whether in Knin or otherwise, let alone at a time when Golubic was closed and Dragan was offering his services to the highest bidder. Precisely which town were Dragan and Simatovic advancing on? Why have the Prosecution failed to adduce a single piece of evidence other than an enthusiastic greeting at Kula that suggests Stanisic did in fact send Dragan to Bosnia. A kiss is just a kiss and a hug is just a hug, and meaningful evidence of concerted action in pursuit of crime, something quite, quite different. A further examination of the context leaves the matter in further doubt. As Your Honours will have seen, according to P651, on the 8th of December, 1991, Milosevic and Karadzic nominated Stanisic as the man to sit down with ten men from the RSK opposition to force Babic's hand. A role which is extended to 44 commanders in January 1992. And yet according to this allegedly authentic intercept Stanisic was simultaneously conducting operations with Dragan as well as with the Red Berets, as well as with Arkan, and well as Skorpions, and so on and so forth, in the Krajina and the SBWS. It is illogical and obviously so. In our respectful submission that short analysis is the type of analysis that this case deserves. The burden and standard of proof is high. It is wholly unsatisfactory to rely upon evidence only because if looked through narrowed eyes and without any context it prejudices the accused. We submit an analysis of this evidence reveals a manifest lack of reliability which, when combined with the evidence of Stanisic's contributions to peace leads to a reasonable conclusion that Stanisic lacked criminal intent. Why was it that Stanisic was chosen to negotiate with Mladic for the release of the UNPROFOR hostages? As we detail in Annex 2 of our closing brief, this was reportedly one of the most sensitive crisis in the Balkans. The Prosecution can do as they might to diminish the value of this act by suggesting Stanisic's motives were not pure but it does not deal with the central question. Why him? Why not Perisic, who, as we know, had an intimate relationship with Mladic? Why not a myriad of other men? No one can seriously suggest that Mladic, the commander of thousands of VRS troops was fearful of Stanisic or his JATD. No evidence exists that Stanisic had an ongoing relationship with Mladic, let alone one of intimacy or affection. The Prosecution claimed yesterday that the -- the fact that Stanisic was able to go and negotiate that release shows he had significant influence, but over who? As the Mladic diary show, he only met Mladic in July 1993 and in 1995 they had not even exchanged phone numbers. So why Stanisic? We suggest the answer lies in the character of the man. It's the same answer to the question why in 1991 and 1992 was Stanisic apparently engaged with persuading the RSK leadership to sign the Vance Plan.
