That answer may help to understand why Stanisic, from 1991 when madness swirled around the Balkans, continued to cultivate relationship with pivotal intelligence services from aboard. Or why as the chief of state security he was chosen to negotiate Dayton? Or why after Dayton, he helped to secure the safety of ongoing peace operations. We refer Your Honours to Annex 2 of our closing brief. You don't have to take my word for it, Your Honours. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why is it that Stanisic did not join Milosevic's party at any time during the indictment period. Why is it that he was against members of the DB joining any political party? Why is it that most DB centres had a multi-ethnic composition? Why was it that not a single Muslim was removed from his service during the war? Why did he allow Zlatko Radnic, a Croat, to remain chief of the 6th Administration throughout the war? We invite you to look at Annex 2 of our brief. You will see this to be undoubtedly true. Radnic was still employed in 1996 and accompanied Stanisic on high-level visits abroad. The Prosecution asks you to ignore these assessments as Stanisic as a non-political and moderate man provided by men of integrity and worth and instead accept the evidence of unsavory characters such as JF-039 or JF-047 who couldn't decide wether he was in an RSK MUP unit or a Serbian MUP unit; or witnesses like Kovacevic or JF-005 who may still be looking for their notes in their kitchen cupboards; or the incorrigible Theunens with his expressions of gratitude for his long-standing employment with the Prosecution at the ICTY. Mr. Stanisic was a pragmatist, not a nationalist or an extremist. He had a job to do that involved at its core as we outline in Annex 1 of our brief to oppose all forms of extreme nationalist activity in order to prevent an intra-national conflict, a civil war and terrorism. Why could a Croat remain in such a high position in the DB and yet that was impossible for other state organs? Because this states organ was not prosecuting a war against Croats, and unlike other state organs, having an ethnically diverse membership was an asset to its work. As I noted at the outset, Stanisic did not believe in a Greater Serbia, depending upon expanding land or territory. As early as 1992 if not before, Stanisic knew that it was not possible to hold Yugoslavia together, let alone achieve the more grandiose ambitions of the nationalists and extremists within Serbia. Not to be shown to the public, please, slide 63 and 64. This is a conversation Stanisic had with Karadzic which we say provides another insight into his mind. From early on in this terrible war, a position he took on the 5th of January, 1992. Karadzic was excited about a speech he had given at a convention that was televised. Stanisic watched the speech and spoke to Karadzic. Stanisic was guarded in his praise of the convention and Karadzic's speech. He did not say he liked. He said that he observed that others did: "We were watching you carefully and that applause you got." Whereas Karadzic characterises his speech as non-elitist, Stanisic is careful to note that he, Karadzic, is "Orthodox," clearly a euphemism for "extreme." He notes that it is the Orthodox leftist that got most from it. Finally, Karadzic notes that he wants "Yugoslavia as a whole," Stanisic notes that he is "wondering the same thing" but finally notes that he does not know how this would be possible. I suggest that this shows, or is at least some evidence of, Stanisic, the pragmatist who knew that it was not possible. In his own quiet way he tried to urge Karadzic to be realistic. Stanisic knew the world didn't work like that. Even if dyed-in-the-wool nationalists like Babic, Martic, Hadzic and Karadzic did not, he knew that this political aim was impossible even though he had to be circumspect when speaking to Karadzic. If that's right or might be right what was Mr. Stanisic's political objective? How could he have thrown himself into prosecuting a war when he did not share a belief in political objectives or share a belief that they were possible? How could he have thrown himself into committing crimes considered by others to be integral to the achievement of their unified Yugoslavia if he doubted from early on that it was not possible? How could he have shared that criminal intent? As the Balkans erupted, Stanisic's job was to prevent Serbia erupting too. His job was critical. Others were perfectly capable and militarily trained to direct and organise the formation of special units, to finance, train and provide logistical support to those special units as well as leading them into battle in furtherance of crimes. Thank you very much for time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It would help if Your Honours saw it but I know the Prosecution object to that so I'll try and do it without. When we went through the Prosecution brief, we noted a number of problems, ranging from citations which were not accurate, just simple errors, which we wanted to correct. We also noted citations which purport to provide corroborative evidence which did not. Problems with relying upon evidence which was not corroborative which had to be 92 quater evidence where the Prosecution hadn't assisted Your Honours in identifying what they say could corroborate, citations to evidence which simply wasn't there, and we took the view that there were certain problems which we were duty bound to raise and to put into a document which we felt would assist Your Honours and your legal officers in expediting the process of assessing the Prosecution's closing brief and assisting Your Honours in the ascertainment of the truth. What we did was, we identified the problems and then went through those problems and removed those problems which we felt amounted to fresh advocacy and limited our comments or corrections to those which we felt, that, if we didn't, there was a possibility that errors in the assessment of evidence might be made. utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good evening to everyone in and around the courtroom. In the entire course of these proceedings and also in their final trial brief and closing arguments, the Prosecution maintained that the JCE was conceived for the purpose to permanently remove the non-Serb population by the use of force from large areas in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and that during that campaign of persecution, Franko Simatovic was one of the more prominent members of the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecution goes onto maintain that this plan originated not earlier than April 1991 and lasted until not later than December 1995. The Prosecution designates Simatovic as Stanisic's deputy and the operative commander of the units of the State Security Service, ignoring, I would say, a great deal of evidence that, to say the least, cast a doubt over such a conclusion. Proceeding from these premises, the Prosecution alleges that Simatovic, occupying the said positions, planned and carried out the joint criminal enterprise, together with the political leaders of the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, their governments, military and police officials, as well as political, military and police leaders of the Republic of Serbia. In their final trial brief, however, the Prosecution states that, beginning with summer 1990, started to assist and advise JCE members in the two Serbian Autonomous Regions in Croatia. The Prosecution also alleges that beginning with summer 1991, JCE members, including the unit that belonged to the DB of Serbia, the Red Berets, as well as Arkan's Serbian Volunteer Guard, the SDG, intimidated and assaulted non-Serb population throughout Serbian Autonomous Regions in Croatia. The Prosecution claims that this pattern from Croatia was applied also in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the JCE members formed parallel institutions and forces, in order to carry out a violent campaign of persecution in the way that had begun in Croatia. The main piece of evidence on which the Prosecution relies for all these allegations is the speech read out by Simatovic before Chief Stanisic, President Milosevic, and other officials at the ceremony in Kula in 1997. Although the evidence that has been led is in stark contrast with the content of the speech read out by Simatovic, the Prosecution relies on this speech as on a central piece of evidence in their case against Simatovic, despite the fact that, as the Defence maintains, the said speech was delivered under particular circumstances and for particular reasons that we will address in due course. It is obvious that after the conclusion of the Dayton Accords in November 1995 the State Security Service of Serbia had particular reasons to present to President Milosevic its own role in the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia in a different light. There is a wealth of evidence that we will shortly emphasise to prove that the assertions made in this speech are inaccurate, exaggerating the role of the RDB of Serbia. To quote an example, the speech refers to 26 locations, allegedly training camps. In these proceedings we had occasion to hear of only several locations where training centres were allegedly established. The same can be said of the reference to 50 locations where the unit allegedly participated in combat operations, as well as the reference to 5.000 unit members who participated in the fighting. After more than three years of hearing a large number of witnesses, and considering all the evidence led, I don't think anyone in this courtroom could count more than five locations to which -- with which the unit for anti-terrorist operations of the State Security Service of Serbia could be associated or where they could possibly have been involved in some operations. The number of 5.000 unit members is absurd in itself, and is deeply discrepant with all the evidence. One glaring example of such exaggeration are allegations about the so-called air squadron which the key witness of the Prosecution, Milovanovic, qualified as inaccurate, and the same applies to the airport used by these alleged aircraft. It is a fact that Franko Simatovic, when reading the speech, whose author we do not know, uses the word "we," but that fact does not mean that he was directly, or in any other way, involved from the very beginning in all the alleged activities of the service. Simatovic is not a synonym for the service, nor is the service a synonym for Simatovic. Whichever employee of the State Security Service of Serbia read out that speech instead of him, he would have had to use the word "we." The Defence believes that the Prosecution was required to lead specific evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the concrete participation of Simatovic for every one of these allegations, if they treat this speech as crown evidence of Simatovic's participation and responsibility. We will further address the most striking evidence that enables the Defence to state that the Prosecution failed to prove Simatovic's criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution claims that Simatovic's speech is an admission and testimony about the events by a direct participant. We believe, after considering the entire body of facts, that the speech does not corroborate the allegations and is not consistent with the evidence and constitutes an exaggerated picture of the State Security Service and its role. The Prosecution claims that Simatovic armed, controlled and commanded some of the direct perpetrators. It is also claimed that materiel, logistical and intelligence support was provided by him to implement the planned JCE. It is claimed, also, that Milosevic, in 1994, estimated that the provided equipment and weapons are in the value of 1 billion dollars. If, indeed, the supplied assistance was worth more than 1 billion dollars, it is unclear from the evidence led by the Prosecution what specific influence and contribution Franko Simatovic had in supplying that money or part of that money. What kind of decision Simatovic made? Whom did he consult? Who informed him? What type of assistance will be extended and in what amount? Which part of that 1 billion dollars was supplied by Simatovic? How much of that assistance can be connected with Simatovic in any way? Is that 1.000 dollars, 100.000 dollars? Is there any evidence of that in this case? Is there any proof? Is there any proof as to what assistance is associated with the DB, what is state assistance, what is JNA assistance, what is assistance from the Army of Yugoslavia? Where exactly is the position of Franko Simatovic in the decision to extent this assistance to the -- to the population, to the Serbian population outside of Serbia, if any? What is his role in the decision-making about providing this assistance? What is the extent of his contribution? There is no evidence of that. There is, however, strong proof that Simatovic had no influence on any possible decisions and any possible assistance to anyone. The Prosecution tries to identify Simatovic with the service or the state of Serbia, which is absolutely inaccurate and unacceptable. The Prosecution failed to present to this Trial Chamber the only relevant evidence; that is to say, evidence as to what, and how much, Simatovic assisted in the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise, if he did so at all. And what is the importance and the consequences of his activities? It is the position of the Defence that the Prosecution was required to point out precisely the specific contribution of Simatovic as a member of the JCE and the extent of his contribution. With all due respect, the Prosecution has failed to do that. In their final trial brief, the Prosecution refers to an integrated network of secret training camps run allegedly by the accused. There is nothing to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused set up and ran an integrated network of secret training camps and ran them. First of all, the Prosecution failed to show what this integrated network of camps consists of. What is it? What is that structure of control or any other element that makes these camps integrated? Thus, for instance, the camp on Mount Tara was established on the orders of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, for the advanced training of PJP members. That camp was in no way secret. PJP, from the public security sector, were trained there. There is evidence of that and we have heard numerous witnesses testifying to that, as we pointed out in our final trial brief. The camp in Golubic was not set up either by Stanisic or Simatovic, not was it in any way secret or concealed. Golubic existed for several months before the arrival of Captain Dragan in Knin, and the training in Golubic was followed by both the domestic and foreign media. Further on, we will deal with these allegations in greater detail. Even if the JCE existed with the objective alleged by the Prosecution, the Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Simatovic participated in that enterprise. The Prosecution did, indeed, enumerate a large number of persons who allegedly were involved in the JCE but failed to prove the existence of any connection or interaction of Simatovic with a large number of these persons who are said to be JCE members. Concerning the persons that Simatovic did have some connection with, the Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Simatovic voluntarily shared the alleged common intent that was the purpose of the JCE. We say that the Prosecution did not provide a single piece of evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Franko Simatovic had any contact with Slobodan Milosevic, first of all, who is considered as the principal JCE member before 1997 at the ceremony in Kula where President Milosevic was present and when there was absolutely no contact between him around Simatovic. Furthermore, there is no evidence provided by the Prosecution of any Simatovic's particular contacts with Kadijevic; Radmilo Bogdanovic; Goran Hadzic; Blagoje Adzic; Radovan Stojicic, Badza; Biljana Plavsic; Momcilo Krajisnik; Mico Stanisic; or Seselj. All that the Prosecution offers as evidence that Simatovic was part of the joint criminal enterprise are two photographs, two entries from the Mladic's diary, and two intercepts with the unsubstantiated and vague theory on the, quote/unquote, close relationship between Simatovic and Stanisic. The Simatovic Defence will, first of all, detail with what the Prosecution calls, quote/unquote, close relationship between Simatovic and Stanisic. The Prosecution does not explain the exact distinction that characterises the official relationship between the chief of the service and one of the employees of the service, and where and how their relationship turns into a close one. It is true, and it is normal, that there was co-operation as there had to be between the chief and his employee who, later on, becomes his advisor. However, the boundary of co-operation, as envisaged by the rules of the service, was never crossed, nor did the Prosecution offer any evidence that the relationship between Stanisic and Simatovic went beyond the rules that both of then had to observe. As regards the said two photographs, that the Prosecution refers to in their final trial brief, the Defence kindly asks the Trial Chamber that these two photographs, P390 and P391, be compared with photograph P3043, which has been in disputably established to have been made at the time of the liberation of hostages in Bosnia in 1994. It is perfectly clear that these two photographs were made at the same time, on the same occasion. The Defence has offered to the Trial Chamber a photograph of Franko Simatovic from spring 1993, where it is clearly seen that Franko Simatovic looks completely different and still wears no glasses. That is Exhibit D862 to which we draw your attention. The statement of Witness Milovanovic that he thinks that the photograph, P390, was made in Belgrade, cannot be relied on as evidence because it is obvious that Milovanovic is only guessing. So much about photographs. As regards the entries in Ratko Mladic's diary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to fully understand, where you said: "It is perfectly clear that these photographs, these two photographs, were made at the same time on the same occasion." Did you intend to say that P390 and P391 were made at the same time and at the same occasion as P3043? Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When I say "at the same time," I should have said "at or around the same time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, what my concern was is you said these two photographs but what you are doing is you are comparing two photographs with a third one, and apparently you want to say that they are made at the same time, approximately, as the other one. Now, I'm still a bit puzzled by your last observation. If you say it's approximately the same time could that then be the same occasion? Because for me, an occasion is limited in time. You said, "at the same time on the same occasion," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, and it is the submission of the Defence that the negotiations on the liberation of hostages took a while, and these photographs were made at the time of the negotiations to liberate the hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not necessarily at the same occasion, that is, the negotiations to liberate the hostages. Or was it at those negotiations that the two photographs were taken? Perhaps you -- you re-read the -- my questions, and we'll then further hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is our submission that they were made during the negotiations. That is what we assert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards Mladic and his diaries, the Defence should like to remind the Trial Chamber that Mladic kept them from 1991 through 1996. In all this time, Mladic noted hundreds of meetings involving a large number of persons, including many meetings with the alleged members of the joint criminal enterprise. In their more than five years while Mladic was noting down all these meetings, he noted Simatovic's presence at some of these meetings only twice. However, in both these cases, Simatovic did not participate in the talks at all. In addition, the Defence wishes to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the first entry dated 28 February 1993 is an entry related to the Operation Udar, Strike, that we will deal with shortly. The second entry, P2541, dated 9 September 1995, is an entry from a meeting of General Mladic, General Perisic and Jovica Stanisic, attended also by Franko Simatovic. The only person who doesn't speak at the meeting is Franko Simatovic. Also telling, if you look at this entry in its entirety, is that this meeting is about the liberation of two foreign pilots, and that was the only topic discussed there. Thus, we have two meetings. No contribution to the discussion. One meeting dealing with the liberation of two foreign pilots. We will provide further explanation of the second meeting shortly. As regards the intercepts, the Defence would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the following: The first intercept mentioning Simatovic is P693. In paragraph 117 of their final trial brief, the Prosecution quotes only the end of this conversation. In order to gain a real picture of this conversation, one has to take into account the whole. One essential thing about this conversation is that it happened by chance. Simatovic just happened to be at the office of Mihajl Kertes at the time when he got a call from President Karadzic. If you take a close look at this intercept, you will see that Karadzic obviously does not recognise Simatovic's voice, that Kertes tells Karadzic that a friend wants to hear him, which is obvious from the B/C/S transcript of this intercept. The content of this conversation between Simatovic and Karadzic does not allow us to make any conclusions about the topic of the conversation. It is also important to note that Simatovic and Karadzic are not on first-name terms. And it's also clear that Karadzic does not recognise Simatovic's voice. Simatovic first introduces himself to Karadzic. Any conclusion beyond a reasonable doubt as to the topic of this conversation and the nature of the relationship between Simatovic and Karadzic, based on this conversation, is absolutely impossible. It is only possible to speculate, and that is precisely what the Prosecution does in their final brief. The second intercept, P671, shows absolutely nothing. This intercept relates to the intercepted conversation between Jovica Stanisic, then chief of the State Security Service of Serbia, with Karadzic, and, in that conversation, Stanisic says: "You have greetings from Frenki and the captain." First of all, this quote does not prove anything, does not show anything. It does not show any connection between Simatovic and Karadzic, except that perhaps they know each other. We don't even know who "the captain" at that office is. That is what the Prosecution offers us as essential, strong proof that Franko Simatovic has a special and a close relationship with a large number of JCE members. We do not believe that this evidence could be sufficient to any reasonable trier of fact to make such a conclusion. In addition, the Prosecution failed to prove the other second cumulative element of the JCE that would prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Simatovic was part of a common plan with a clearly defined role of his own in that plan. Another standard accepted before this Tribunal and another thing that the Prosecution has to prove. As for the mental elements of JCE, the Defence emphasises that, in this case file, there is no direct evidence on Simatovic's state of mind. The only piece of evidence that contains something relevant to what we could call Simatovic's state of mind is his own statement concerning the -- the speech in Kula, is his speech in Kula. However, that is a speech that Simatovic only read out on behalf of the service, on behalf of the State Security Service of Serbia, with all the shortcomings that we have already addressed and described in greater detail in our brief. That evidence on the existence of JCE and Simatovic's participation in it is unreliable and insufficient to prove it beyond a reasonable doubt. It's also obvious from the examples uses [as interpreted] to corroborate their allegations in their final brief. We have no doubt that the Trial Chamber shall consider all of the evidence presented by both the Prosecution and the Defence in a detailed way and in all its aspects. We only wish to point out here to some examples of misinterpretation of evidence by the Prosecution and their reliance on evidence of little or no probative value or evidence that is insufficient to prove the Prosecution theory beyond a reasonable doubt. When analysing the implementation of JCE in SAO Krajina, the Prosecution relies heavily on the testimony of Witness Babic, who testified in the Milosevic case, and whose testimony the Defence of Franko Simatovic never had an occasion to test through cross-examination. This witness assesses the role and participation of Simatovic in the events of the summer of 1991 in a very superficial and generalised way, in P1878. From the evidence offered by the Prosecution, it is completely impossible to see the specific role of Simatovic in setting up the police stations in Krajina. The Defence had no opportunity to examine the witness on this issue, which strips -- which strips this evidence of all its probative value. Furthermore, the Prosecution claims that in January 1991, Martic agreed with Bogdanovic and Stanisic about the provision of material, technical and monetary assistance to Krajina, wherein Simatovic would supply salaries, uniforms and equipment for special police. Maintaining this allegation, the Prosecution invokes the testimony of JF-039. At this moment, Your Honours, could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 31st of January, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in this same courtroom, III.
